\chapter{Inside the House}
\label{ch:gu-inside-the-house}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear and say five everyday Gujarati household words, and read and write one of them.}

Five household words enter meaning-first by ear, one lesson each; an oral checkpoint scores listening and speaking apart, window reaches the page with signs taught before chapter 8, and an R1 return carries the chapter-17 family words back at their fourth spacing window.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bārṇũ]{\gu{બારણું} — hear door}

\label{lesson:GU-C28-hear-baarnun}



\begin{quote}
Say the Gujarati word for home, from the first three-place map. Now listen twice: \textbf{bārṇũ}. It means \textbf{door} — the one you open to come in, and listen to that ending: the nasalized \emph{-ũ} that marks a neuter word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bārṇũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bārṇũ\textquotedblright{} twice, once slowly and once at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bārṇũ} mean? (\textbf{Door.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/door}{Cambridge: door}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bārī]{\gu{બારી} — hear window}

\label{lesson:GU-C28-hear-baari}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for door. Now listen twice: \textbf{bārī}. It means \textbf{window} — the same opening in a wall, only smaller, and one sound away from \emph{bārṇũ}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bārī\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bārṇũ\textquotedblright{} for door, then \textquotedblleft{}bārī\textquotedblright{} for window
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bārī} mean? (\textbf{Window.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/window}{Cambridge: window}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[Practice]{Five things in one house, by ear}

\label{lesson:GU-C28-house-five}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new arrives here. Say the first and the last word of the chapter before any list is read to you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Keep two scores. \textbf{Listening} goes from sound to meaning; \textbf{speaking} goes from meaning to sound. A strong score in one cannot cover a miss in the other. The third row is not new material — it is the five food words of the previous chapter, returning at their second spacing window.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of the five are openings in a wall? (\textbf{bārṇũ} and \textbf{bārī}.)

\section[Practice]{Bārī reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C28-baari}



\begin{quote}
Before anything is uncovered, say the Gujarati word for \textbf{window}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Uncover \textbf{\gu{બારી}} once. Four pieces, none new: \textbf{\gu{બ}} from the forms that come before your name, the \textbf{\gu{ા}} stroke from the greeting, \textbf{\gu{ર}} from the courtesy chapter, and the \textbf{\gu{ી}} sign from the doorway nine. Name the pieces aloud in order, then read the whole word once. This is the only word of the chapter the hand is asked for; the other four stay in the ear for now, which is the gloss-first order rather than an omission.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\gu{બારી}} once. Repair one shape if it needs it; do not start a row.

\subsection*{Your turn — the eight time words at their third window}
The lamp above is lit at \emph{sānj}, so the time words are already in the room. All eight were first written twenty-five and more positions ago; this is their third spacing window, and this row is cold reading, not recall from a list.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four signs in \emph{bārī} came from the doorway nine? (The \textbf{\gu{ી}} — the long-i sign.)

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/window}{Cambridge: window}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The house returns at R1, and the family at R4}

\label{lesson:GU-R28-house-five-r1}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new arrives here. Say the words for door and for lamp before anything is read to you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\textbf{Listening} runs sound to meaning; \textbf{speaking} runs meaning to sound, exactly as they did one lesson ago.

\subsection*{Your turn — the distant band, the friend and the family}
A house holds people as well as furniture. These four were introduced around position 105 and have not been asked for since; at this position they are more than a hundred lessons old, which is the fourth spacing window rather than the third.

\subsection*{Writing — from sound, every model covered}
Record \textbf{writing} on its own; a 5/5 in listening cannot cover a miss here.

Rice reached the page nine lessons ago; this is its second window.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word in the band names the whole group rather than one person? (\textbf{kuṭumb} — the family.)
